name: EVCache
tagline: Netflix's memcached-based distributed cache with zone-aware replication, built for AWS microservices.
description: EVCache (Ephemeral Volatile Cache) is Netflix's distributed caching layer, open-sourced in 2013, made of memcached server clusters plus a Java client library that handles placement and replication. The client shards keys within a zone by Ketama consistent hashing, writes every item to a copy of the cache in each AWS availability zone and reads from the local zone first, so losing a zone costs latency rather than hits; large values are chunked, servers are found through service discovery, and a replication service copies data across regions. Consistency is explicitly best-effort, with failed writes sent to Kafka for a consistency checker to repair. It remains actively maintained, with v5.28 released in September 2026. Outside Netflix-style Java/AWS stacks, a managed Memcached or Redis/Valkey service is usually simpler to adopt.

scale.notes: Client-side sharding across memcached nodes, full replica per availability zone, cross-region replication at Netflix.

strengths: Zone-aware replication: each availability zone holds a full copy, so zone loss does not drop hit rates
Battle-tested at Netflix scale for years
Builds on plain memcached, so server behaviour is simple and well understood
Actively maintained Java client (5.x releases through 2026)
weaknesses: Best-effort consistency: zone copies can diverge until TTL expiry or repair
Client logic is Java-centric; other languages need a proxy or their own implementation
Assumes Netflix-style service discovery and AWS availability zones
Cache only: no persistence guarantees or rich data types like Redis
useCases: Multi-zone caching in front of databases for Java microservices on AWS
Session and personalisation data with short TTLs
Read-heavy caches with sub-millisecond in-zone latency targets
